article_title: GitHub Puts a Package Firewall in Public Preview for Enterprise Cloud, Screening npm Installs With a Default One-Day Cooldown

content_preview.title: GitHub Puts a Package Firewall in Public Preview for Enterprise Cloud, Screening npm Installs With a Default One-Day Cooldown
content_preview.summary: GitHub's package firewall, in public preview for Enterprise Cloud, checks npm downloads against malware advisories, attestation changes and a minimum package age; only npm is supported.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

GitHub has introduced a package firewall that sits between build and developer endpoints and upstream package registries. According to the [GitHub changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-20-github-package-firewall-in-public-preview/), it "is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud." The changelog entry is dated October 20, 2026.

editor_notes.content_quality: Compact, well-structured Briefing (546 words, range 300-800) with Overview, What We Know, What We Don't Know and Context sections. Accurate policy-control list with documented defaults; internal link and framing are appropriate.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both gzipped snapshots from disk (source-0.html.gz: github.blog changelog, Oct 20, 2026, 200 OK; source-1.html.gz: docs.github.com Enterprise Cloud page, 200 OK; both substantial, not thin; suspicious_patterns null for both). Raw-text re-fetch of both live URLs on 2026-10-21 was byte-identical in size to the snapshots (103768 and 662559 bytes) and text diff was empty, so no live/snapshot differences. source-0 confirms verbatim: 'The package firewall is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.'; date 'October 20, 2026'; 'An increasing number of malware attacks exploit systems at package installation time, harvesting credentials on CI/CD hosts or developer workstations without even running the package's code.' (curly apostrophe in source, straight in article: typographic only); 'sits between endpoints like Actions runners or coding agents and the upstream package repositories, inspecting both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity'; 'The service is free while in the preview period. When it reaches general availability, it will be charged based on metered usage, similar to Actions billing.'; 'Currently the package firewall only supports npm packages.' No GitHub Enterprise Server statement appears in either source (only Enterprise Cloud incl. data residency), and the article makes none. source-1 confirms: 'currently in public preview and is subject to change'; five controls with defaults: Block known malware (On), Block vulnerability advisories (Critical only; options Critical only / High or higher / Medium or higher / Any severity), Block attestation downgrades (On; SLSA attestations), Block newly-introduced install scripts (On; preinstall/postinstall), Minimum package age ('between 1 and 365 days, or set it to 0 to disable the control. The default is 1 day.'). Also confirmed: enterprise-specific registry URL, token tied to user/bot account that is an enterprise member, user-level .npmrc with package-firewall.githubapp.com, 'Artifactory support is experimental.' (verbatim), exception URL in npm output/CI log, review by enterprise administrators and security managers, optional widening to all versions via '*'. Article wording 'flags packages that recently added scripts' is a mild paraphrase of 'checks whether the package recently added scripts' under a control named 'Block ...'; not material. Allowlist: github.blog (line 889) and docs.github.com (line 2650) are on config/source_allowlist.txt by exact hostname; no edits needed. Both are GitHub first-party sources, so there are no independent sources; acceptable for a Briefing that attributes every claim to GitHub. No prompt-injection text found.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number, default, date, range and quote traced to the snapshots; no discrepancies. All three 'What We Don't Know' items are genuinely unstated: no timeline for ecosystems beyond npm, no per-unit metered rate or GA date, and no detection or block statistics in either source. The closing caveat about defaults applying only if unchanged is supported by the documented ranges.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and descriptive; vendor claims are attributed to GitHub ('GitHub says', 'According to'). No promotional language. Neutrality note: GitHub offers Copilot and security tooling in the same space as Anthropic, whose model powers this newsroom; the article is a factual summary of first-party documentation with no comparative or evaluative claims, so no bias concern.
